newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan fiscal reform may be all bark and no bite.
newsitem.headline: Japan fiscal reform may be all bark and no bite.

text.p: A campaign by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto to put the nation's debt-ridden finances in order may end up as a numbers game and turn out to be all bark and no bite.

A government panel headed by Hashimoto released an interim report earlier this week seeking drastic cuts in spending, in another sign of his pledge to slash the government deficit to three percent or less of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2003.

Japan's fiscal deficit for calendar 1997 is forecast at about 6.3 percent of GDP, one of the highest levels among major industrialised countries, and Hashimoto has stressed the need to overhaul the structure of Japan's finances.
But the cuts, aimed at keeping next year's general expenditures below this year's levels, are still far from achieving fiscal "structural reform", economists said.

"There is a danger that this may end up just being a temporary makeshift reform," said Naozumi Atoda, a professor at Osaka University and a member of a group of academics urging overall fiscal reform.
The government panel called for cuts in major areas of spending, including those traditionally considered as "sanctuaries", such as public works, defence and agriculture.
Finance Ministry mandarins, eager to capitalise on any chance to cut budget spending, applauded the panel's report.
"The report set the way for the government to tackle overall structural reforms without exception," said Vice Finance Minister Tadashi Ogawa.
The panel plans to come up with a final report by the end of this month, incorporating numerical targets for the cuts.
But economists said the measures, even if accompanied by specific targets, would be merely superficial and lacked vision on how to reform the present fiscal structure.

In many areas, the report said, annual spending should be decreased by extending the length of a spending programme covering a certain number of years while keeping the total amount of spending of the programme unchanged.

"The extension will not lead to changes in policy priorities or the present fiscal structure. We must not forget that the real aim of fiscal reform is not just cutting down spending or the state deficit," said Atsushi Miyawaki, a Hokkaido University professor belonging to the academic group.
"Priorities (on spending) should be given according to the effectiveness of a policy," added Osaka University's Atoda.
Agricultural assistance and public works have come under fire for eating up the state budget but being ineffective.
Criticism has especially mounted over a six-year 6.1 trillion yen ($52.5 billion) programme to help farmers cope with competition from imports resulting from the Uruguay Round trade agreement.

There have been reports that some municipal governments alloted with the funds for the programme have been at a loss on what to do with the money and used it for projects straying from the original purpose, such as building lodging facilities to attract tourists.
"We must look at the outcome of policy, not just the output," said Atoda.
Hashimoto's efforts may also be crippled by opposition from politicians within his very own party, seeking to protect the interests of those expected to be hit by the planned cuts.

"We must take plenty of time and not rush (at fiscal reform). To seek cuts across the board in all areas of spending lack principle," said Tokuichiro Tamazawa, head of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party's (LDP) agricultural committee.

Although Tamazawa said the committee agreed with the prime minister's plan to cut annual spending on the Uruguay Round related assistance, he added that there was still strong demand to strengthen social infrastructure in rural areas.
"Japan may have gotten rich, but in some farm towns, they didn't even have a sewerage system until recently," he said.
Voices of politicians such as Tamazawa, who represent the interests of farmers, carry weight within the LDP as farmers make up the party's main support base.

If the panel is able to ride through the political wrangling and issue its final report, the government plans to incorporate it into a fiscal reform bill to be submitted to parliament sometime in the autumn. ($1=116 yen)
